claim: The study included 23 participants who completed the full 3-day experimental paradigm.
source: The final sample consisted of 23 right-handed participants (mean age = 22.91 years, SD = 5.03, range 18–35; 14 females) with normal or corrected-to-normal vision and no self-reported history of psychiatric or neurological disorders.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the final sample size and participant characteristics in the Methods section.

claim: Nine participants dropped out before completing the 3-day study.
source: Nine dropped out before completing the 3-day study (two felt motion sick, two experienced unrelated illness, and five did not want to continue past Day 1), and data from one participant were excluded for failing to respond during the fMRI task.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the number and reasons for participant dropout.

claim: Participants completed two behavioral navigation tasks interspersed between 3 consecutive days of fMRI.
source: Participants (n = 23) completed two behavioral navigation tasks interspersed between 3 consecutive days of fMRI (Figure 1a).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental design and references Figure 1a showing the paradigm structure.

claim: The virtual environment consisted of three oval tracks of distinct texture and color.
source: The virtual environment contained three oval-shaped tracks of distinct texture and color (Figure 1b).
evidence: The manuscript describes the virtual environment structure and references Figure 1b showing the environment.

claim: Each track contained five goal locations marked by unique fractal images.
source: Individual tracks contained five goals, initially marked by unique fractal images.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the number and marking of goal locations.

claim: Each track had one landmark in common with each of the other two tracks.
source: Importantly, each track had one landmark in common with each of the other two tracks.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the shared landmark structure across tracks.

claim: Participants were not aware that the tracks would be connected prior to the start of the Global Task.
source: Participants were not informed and not aware that the tracks would be connected prior to the start of the Global Task, despite the shared landmarks.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states participants' lack of awareness about track connectivity.

claim: During the Local Navigation Task, participants navigated to the correct location on 96% of trials across Day 1 test trials.
source: Across Day 1 test trials, participants navigated to the correct location on 96% of trials, with performance close to ceiling from the beginning of testing (Figure 2a, top).
evidence: The manuscript reports the accuracy data and references Figure 2a showing performance.

claim: Local Navigation Task accuracy was significantly above chance level.
source: The proportion of correct trials was significantly above chance (0.25, or 1 of 4 possible goals; mean ± SEM: 0.961 ± 0.009; t22 = 82.831, one-sample t-test; p < 2.2e–16, d = 17.27)
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical test results comparing accuracy to chance level.

claim: Local Navigation Task accuracy on Day 2 did not differ from that on the final Day 1 test run.
source: Accuracy on Day 2 (mean ± SEM: 0.985 ± 0.004) did not differ from that on the final Day 1 test run (t22 = 1.418; p = 0.17, paired t-test).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison of accuracy across days.

claim: Path inefficiency improved across the four learning runs during Local Navigation.
source: During Local Navigation (Figure 2a, bottom), path inefficiency improved across the four learning runs (effect of run, β = –8.99 ± 1.262; t = –7.125; p < 1.34e–12; d = 1.49)
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis showing improvement in path efficiency over learning runs.

claim: During the Global Navigation Task, within-track accuracy was higher than across-track accuracy.
source: During Global Navigation, within-track accuracy was higher than across-track accuracy (t20 = 4.073; p = 0.0006, paired t-test; d = 0.89).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison of accuracy between trial types.

claim: Across-track accuracy showed a trend towards increasing across test runs during Global Navigation.
source: However, across-track accuracy showed a trend towards increasing across test runs (effect of run, β = 0.007 ± 0.004; t = 1.792; p = 0.073; no effect of run on within-track trials, β = –0.005 ± 0.004; t = –1.103; p = 0.27)
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis showing a trend in accuracy improvement.

claim: Accuracy significantly improved overnight for both within-track and across-track trials between Day 2 and Day 3.
source: Accuracy significantly improved overnight for both trial types (within-track mean ± SEM: 0.963 ± 0.013, t20 = 2.425, p = 0.025, paired t-test, d = 0.53; across-track mean ± SEM: 0.929 ± 0.025, t20 = 2.841, p = 0.01, paired t-test, d = 0.62)
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparisons showing overnight improvement.

claim: Navigation was significantly more inefficient on across-track vs. within-track trials during Day 2 test runs.
source: Similarly, on Day 2 test runs, navigation was significantly more inefficient on across-track (mean ± SEM: 37.86 ± 6.389%) vs. within-track trials (mean ± SEM: 23.479 ± 5.764%; t20 = 3.215, paired t-test; p = 0.004; d = 0.70).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison of path inefficiency between trial types.

claim: There were striking individual differences in path inefficiency when navigating across tracks in the Global Navigation Task on Day 2.
source: Examination of performance at the participant level revealed striking individual differences in path inefficiency when navigating across tracks in the Global Navigation Task on Day 2 (range = 4.219–107.237%, Q1 = 17.914%, Q3 = 54.625%; Figure 6a).
evidence: The manuscript reports descriptive statistics showing variability in performance and references Figure 6a.

claim: Right hippocampus differentiates landmarks located on the same track following Global Navigation.
source: As a priori predicted, we found evidence in right hippocampus that learning differentiates landmarks located on the same track (Day 3 > Day 1 × context, β = –0.013 ± 0.007; t = –2.014; p = 0.044, did not survive FDR correction; d = 0.44; Figure 3a; Appendix 1—Tables 2–3).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results and references Figure 3a showing the effect.

claim: Left EC differentiates items located on the same track following Local Navigation.
source: As predicted, we observed an interaction between context and scan in left EC (Day 2 > Day 1 × context, β = –0.014 ± 0.006; t = –2.339; p = 0.019, did not survive FDR correction; d = 0.52; Figure 3c; Appendix 1—table 7), such that similarity for same-track vs. across-track items did not differ Pre-Learning, but same-track items were less similar (differentiated) following Local Navigation.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results and references Figure 3c showing the effect.

claim: Hippocampal patterns for nearest neighboring landmarks were differentiated following both Local and Global Navigation.
source: As a priori predicted, we found significant interactions between distance and scan (Day 2 > Day 1 × distance, β = 0.04 ± 0.015; t = 2.70; p = 0.007, fell near FDR-corrected threshold (p = 0.005), d = 0.56; Day 3 > Day 1 × distance, β = 0.034 ± 0.015; t = 2.259; p = 0.024; did not survive FDR correction; d = 0.49; Appendix 1—table 11), such that following the Local and Global Tasks, hippocampal patterns were less similar (differentiated) for nearby landmarks vs. landmarks located further apart (Figure 4b).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results and references Figure 4b showing the effect.

claim: Hippocampal pattern similarity for locations across tracks was higher for closer vs. farther locations Post Local Navigation.
source: Consistent with our prediction, we found an interaction between link distance and scan following the Local Task (Day 2 > Day 1 × distance, β = –0.02 ± 0.007; t = –2.891; p = 0.004, survived FDR correction; d = 0.60), but not the Global Task (Day 3 > Day 1 × distance, β = –0.003 ± 0.007; t = –0.413; p = 0.679; Figure 5b; Appendix 1—table 14).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results and references Figure 5b showing the effect.

claim: There was a significant interaction between path inefficiency and link distance in hippocampal pattern similarity Post Local Navigation.
source: Indeed, we observed a significant interaction between path inefficiency and link distance (β = –0.001 ± 0.001; t = –1.983; p = 0.048, did not survive FDR correction; d = 0.43; Appendix 1—table 24), but the direction of the effect was unexpected.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results relating neural patterns to behavior.

claim: Participants who did well from the beginning of the Global Task showed no effect of distance in hippocampal pattern similarity, whereas less efficient navigators showed a negative slope.
source: Participants who did well from the beginning of the Global Task showed no effect of distance in hippocampal pattern similarity, whereas less efficient navigators showed a negative slope (Figure 6b).
evidence: The manuscript describes the pattern of results and references Figure 6b showing the relationship.

claim: There was trend-level evidence that hippocampal pattern similarity Post Local Navigation for landmark pairs predicted trial-level subsequent Global Navigation performance.
source: Here, we observed trend-level evidence that hippocampal pattern similarity (Post Local Navigation) for landmark pairs predicted trial-level subsequent Global Navigation performance (β = –41.245 ± 24.162; t = –1.707; p = 0.088; Appendix 1—table 27), such that greater hippocampal pattern similarity was predictive of a more efficient path (Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results relating neural patterns to subsequent behavior.

claim: The hippocampus plays a critical role in building episodic memories and structured knowledge by binding together inputs from distributed cortical regions.
source: In subserving rapid learning over co-occurring features, the hippocampus plays a critical role in building episodic memories and structured knowledge by binding together inputs from distributed cortical regions, forming conjunctive representations of experiences (McClelland et al., 1995; Teyler and DiScenna, 1986; Libby et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior literature to support this claim about hippocampal function.

claim: Pattern separation is a hypothesized hippocampal mechanism in which the hippocampus creates distinct neural representations for highly similar events.
source: One hypothesized hippocampal mechanism is pattern separation, in which the hippocampus creates distinct neural representations for highly similar events (O'Reilly and McClelland, 1994; Leutgeb et al., 2007; Yassa and Stark, 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior literature to define pattern separation.

claim: Through pattern separation, the hippocampus avoids the blending of similar experiences in memory, reducing across-event interference and forgetting.
source: Through pattern separation, the hippocampus avoids the blending of similar experiences in memory, reducing across-event interference and forgetting.
evidence: The manuscript describes the functional consequence of pattern separation based on theoretical understanding.

claim: fMRI studies have found evidence for pattern separation when experiences have high overlap or lead to similar outcomes.
source: Such studies have found intriguing evidence for pattern separation when experiences have high overlap or lead to similar outcomes (Bakker et al., 2008; Schlichting et al., 2015; Kyle et al., 2015; Ballard et al., 2019), with links to later remembering (LaRocque et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior fMRI studies that found evidence for pattern separation.

claim: Some fMRI studies have found evidence for pattern differentiation, where event overlap appears to trigger a 'repulsion' of hippocampal representations beyond baseline similarity.
source: Moreover, some fMRI studies have found evidence for pattern differentiation, where event overlap appears to trigger a 'repulsion' of hippocampal representations beyond baseline similarity to reduce interference (Wammes et al., 2022; Favila et al., 2016; Chanales et al., 2017; Schapiro et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2017; Jiang et al., 2020; Hulbert and Norman, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior fMRI studies that found evidence for pattern differentiation.

claim: The hippocampus is essential for building structured knowledge and forming cognitive maps that capture relations between spatial, perceptual, and conceptual features.
source: Despite evidence supporting the hippocampus's role in forming distinct memories for events, decades of work also suggest it is essential for building structured knowledge and forming cognitive maps that capture relations between spatial, perceptual, and conceptual features that were encountered in separate events that share common elements (Tolman, 1948; O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; Epstein et al., 2017; Schlichting et al., 2015; Tompary and Davachi, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites decades of prior work to support this claim about hippocampal function.

claim: The hippocampus quickly extracts the temporal structure of an environment as defined by the transition probabilities between items in sequences.
source: For example, the hippocampus quickly extracts the temporal structure of an environment as defined by the transition probabilities between items in sequences (Schapiro et al., 2012; Schapiro et al., 2013)
evidence: The manuscript cites prior studies to support this claim about hippocampal function.

claim: The hippocampus represents higher order structure when there is no variance in transition probabilities between items but an underlying community structure in a sequence.
source: and it represents higher order structure when there is no variance in transition probabilities between items but an underlying community structure in a sequence (Schapiro et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites a prior study to support this claim about hippocampal function.

claim: The hippocampus is essential for inferring indirect relationships between items and events.
source: Moreover, it is essential for inferring indirect relationships between items and events (Schapiro et al., 2014; Zeithamova et al., 2012; Vaidya et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior studies to support this claim about hippocampal function.

claim: Retrieval-based learning, recurrent mechanisms within the episodic memory network, and memory replay enable representational integration.
source: Prior work suggests that retrieval-based learning, recurrent mechanisms within the episodic memory network, and memory replay enable representational integration and allow for the encoding of relationships that have never been directly experienced (Schapiro et al., 2016; Kumaran and McClelland, 2012; Kumaran et al., 2016; Schapiro et al., 2017; Gupta et al., 2010; Wu and Foster, 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work to support this claim about mechanisms of integration.

claim: Integrative encoding is thought to occur when a new experience triggers the recall of a related past episode, and the concurrent activation results in the formation of an integrated representation.
source: For example, integrative encoding is thought to occur when a new experience (BC) triggers the recall of a related past episode (AB), and the concurrent activation of the remembered and presently experienced episodes results in the formation of an integrated representation (ABC) that can support future inference and generalization (Shohamy and Wagner, 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work to describe the mechanism of integrative encoding.

claim: Online replay during periods of awake rest has been shown to integrate multiple events, rather than just replaying a single event.
source: Online replay during periods of awake rest has been shown to integrate multiple events, rather than just replaying a single event (Gupta et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites a prior study to support this claim about replay.

claim: Offline replay during sharp wave-ripples is associated with memory consolidation and updates to neocortical knowledge structures.
source: Offline replay during sharp wave-ripples is associated with memory consolidation and updates to neocortical knowledge structures (Yu et al., 2018; Jadhav et al., 2016; Lewis and Durrant, 2011; Clewett et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior studies to support this claim about offline replay.

claim: Spatial learning is rich with structure and well-suited for exploring the role of differentiation and integration in the formation of local and global knowledge.
source: Spatial learning is rich with structure and thus well-suited for exploring the role of differentiation and integration in the formation of local and global knowledge across experiences.
evidence: The manuscript makes a theoretical argument about the suitability of spatial learning for studying these mechanisms.

claim: A previous study found that representations of routes with overlapping sections were differentiated in the hippocampus following learning.
source: Indeed, a previous study in which participants viewed first-person trajectories to real-world destinations found that representations of routes with overlapping sections were differentiated in the hippocampus following learning (Chanales et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites a prior study to support this claim about route differentiation.

claim: Another study observed differentiation of hippocampal patterns for landmarks that were common to multiple virtual cities.
source: Another study observed differentiation of hippocampal patterns for landmarks that were common to multiple virtual cities (Zheng et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites a prior study to support this claim about landmark differentiation.

claim: Other studies found evidence of integration for items that share spatial and temporal context.
source: By contrast, other studies found evidence of integration for items that share spatial and temporal context (Deuker et al., 2016)
evidence: The manuscript cites a prior study to support this claim about integration.

claim: A study found evidence of integration for objects located in geometrically similar positions across subspaces of segmented environments.
source: and for objects located in geometrically similar positions across subspaces of segmented environments (Peer et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites a prior study to support this claim about integration.

claim: Spatial cells in the hippocampus and EC encode position, head-direction, speed, and other environmental features.
source: Spatial cells in these regions encode position, head-direction, speed, and other environmental features (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; McNaughton et al., 2006; Hafting et al., 2005; Kropff et al., 2015)
evidence: The manuscript cites prior studies to support this claim about spatial cell properties.

claim: Spatial knowledge acquired across learning consists of both local and global representations that are used to different extents based on navigational demands.
source: Spatial knowledge acquired across learning consists of both local and global representations that are used to different extents based on navigational demands (Chrastil, 2013)
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work to support this claim about spatial knowledge.

claim: The study hypothesized that evidence for both integration and differentiation would emerge at the same time points across learning.
source: We hypothesized that we would find evidence for both integration and differentiation emerging at the same time points across learning, as participants build local and global representations of the virtual environment.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the hypothesis.

claim: The study predicted that early evidence of global map learning during local navigation would depend on integration and predict participants' ability to subsequently navigate across the environment.
source: Moreover, we predicted that early evidence of global map learning during local navigation would depend on integration and predict participants' ability to subsequently navigate across the environment.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the prediction.

claim: Both differentiation and integration occur concurrently within the hippocampus and can emerge at the same points in learning.
source: Here, we provide complementary evidence that both differentiation and integration occur concurrently within the hippocampus and can emerge at the same points in learning.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the findings in the Discussion section.

claim: Hippocampal differentiation provides a structure necessary for participants to distinguish between nearby locations.
source: Our data suggest that hippocampal differentiation provides a structure necessary for participants to distinguish between nearby locations, while integration processes serve to build a global map of the environment.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the findings to infer the functional role of differentiation.

claim: Integration processes serve to build a global map of the environment.
source: Our data suggest that hippocampal differentiation provides a structure necessary for participants to distinguish between nearby locations, while integration processes serve to build a global map of the environment.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the findings to infer the functional role of integration.

claim: Integration relates to individual differences in the ability to efficiently navigate between locations in the global map that have not been previously traversed.
source: Moreover, integration relates to individual differences in the ability to efficiently navigate between locations in the global map that have not been previously traversed.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the findings relating neural patterns to behavioral differences.

claim: The findings are consistent with behavioral research examining individual differences in route integration and cognitive map formation.
source: Our findings are consistent with behavioral research examining individual differences in route integration and cognitive map formation. Prior work characterized navigators into groups of 'integrators', 'nonintegrators', and 'imprecise navigators', suggesting that while some individuals build accurate internal maps, others may rely on fragmented maps or route-based strategies during navigation (Weisberg et al., 2014; Weisberg and Newcombe, 2016; Weisberg and Newcombe, 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior behavioral research to contextualize the findings.

claim: The study provides an important extension of prior studies by identifying potential neural substrates of individual differences in cognitive map formation.
source: Importantly, individual differences in navigation inefficiency enabled us to probe variability in neural representations and relate neural pattern similarity to behavior. Our work provides an important extension of prior studies in that it identifies potential neural substrates of individual differences in cognitive map formation.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the contribution of the findings relative to prior work.

claim: Cognitive map formation may not be a 'default' that incidentally emerges during performance of immersive, goal-directed local navigation.
source: Crucially, not all participants demonstrated integration early in the Global Task, suggesting that cognitive map formation may not be a 'default' that incidentally emerges during performance of immersive, goal-directed local navigation.
evidence: The manuscript infers from the behavioral variability observed in the data.

claim: The flat distance-related similarity function observed after global map learning could be a signature of an integrated map.
source: The flat slope observed on Day 3 could thus be a signature of an integrated map.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about the interpretation of the neural pattern.

claim: The hippocampus begins to build a cognitive map extending beyond directly experienced transitions in a goal-directed task.
source: The present study provides complementary evidence that the hippocampus begins to build a cognitive map extending beyond directly experienced transitions in a goal-directed task.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes a key finding of the study.

claim: Overlapping features within the virtual environment provide the hippocampus with the links it needs to begin building a global map.
source: Overlapping features within the virtual environment (the landmarks shared between tracks) provide the hippocampus with the links it needs to begin building a global map, despite participants not yet experiencing the connected environment.
evidence: The manuscript infers the mechanism by which global map building occurs.

claim: Hippocampal differentiation may require extensive learning, potentially including learning that takes place via replay and consolidation processes occurring during sleep.
source: In the present paradigm, fMRI took place 21.5–31 hr after extensive navigational practice, raising the possibility that hippocampal differentiation requires extensive learning, potentially including learning that takes place via replay and consolidation processes occurring during sleep.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about the timing and mechanisms of differentiation.

claim: Fractals are only visible in the environment for a minority of trials during navigation.
source: For example, fractals are only visible in the environment for a minority of trials.
evidence: The manuscript describes a feature of the experimental design.

claim: During the majority of navigation, participants must rely on the landmark buildings to guide them.
source: During the majority of navigation, participants must rely on the landmark buildings to guide them.
evidence: The manuscript infers navigational strategy from the experimental design.

claim: Fractals serve as pointers to the goal location but fractal information may not be used during route planning.
source: Fractals serve as pointers to the goal location to which a participant must navigate on a particular trial, but fractal information may not be used during route planning.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about the role of fractals in navigation.

claim: Local and global maps can be built from landmarks alone.
source: Further, fractals are not necessary for participants to learn the layout of the environment; local and global maps can be built from landmarks alone.
evidence: The manuscript infers the sufficiency of landmarks for map building.

claim: Mnemonic integration depends in part on retrieval and interactions between the hippocampus and vmPFC.
source: Mnemonic integration depends in part on retrieval and interactions between the hippocampus and vmPFC (Zheng et al., 2021; Preston and Eichenbaum, 2013; Kuhl et al., 2012; Zeithamova and Preston, 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work to support this claim about integration mechanisms.

claim: The study did not observe robust effects in vmPFC.
source: In the present work, we did not observe robust effects in vmPFC, but it remains possible that this region may represent features of the environment that were not explicit to our modeling approach.
evidence: The manuscript reports the absence of effects in vmPFC.

claim: Some of the findings do not survive correction for multiple comparisons and should be interpreted with caution.
source: Moreover, some of our findings do not survive correction for multiple comparisons, and thus should be interpreted with caution.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges a limitation of the statistical findings.

claim: The current study was limited in its investigation of individual differences due to sample size.
source: The current study was limited in its investigation of individual differences due to sample size.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges a limitation of the study.

claim: Participants returned 24 hr after Day 1 for Day 2 (range = 21–31.5 hr).
source: After Day 1, participants returned 24 hr (range = 21–31.5 hr) later for Day 2
evidence: The manuscript reports the timing of experimental sessions.

claim: Participants returned 24 hr after Day 2 for Day 3 (range = 15.5–28.5 hr).
source: After Day 2, participants returned 24 hr (range = 15.5–28.5 hr) later for Day 3
evidence: The manuscript reports the timing of experimental sessions.

claim: Navigation was considered accurate if the participant landed within 8 arbitrary units of the goal.
source: Navigation was considered accurate if the participant landed within 8 arbitrary units of the goal (36% of the average distance between goals).
evidence: The manuscript defines the accuracy criterion used in the analysis.

claim: Participants received compensation of $20/hr for their participation.
source: Participants received compensation for their participation ($20/hr).
evidence: The manuscript reports participant compensation.

claim: Whole-brain imaging data were acquired on a 3T GE Discovery MR750 MRI scanner.
source: Whole-brain imaging data were acquired on a 3T GE Discovery MR750 MRI scanner (GE Healthcare) using a 32-channel radiofrequency receive-only head coil (Nova Medical).
evidence: The manuscript describes the MRI acquisition parameters.

claim: Functional data were acquired using a three-band echo planar imaging sequence with 63 oblique axial slices.
source: Functional data were acquired using a three-band echo planar imaging (EPI) sequence (acceleration factor = 2) consisting of 63 oblique axial slices parallel to the long axis of the hippocampus (TR = 1.8 s, TE = 30ms, flip angle = 75°, FOV = 220mm × 220mm, voxel size = 2 × 2 × 2 mm3).
evidence: The manuscript describes the fMRI acquisition parameters.

claim: fMRI data preprocessing was performed with fMRIPrep 1.5.3rc2.
source: fMRI data preprocessing was performed with fMRIPrep 1.5.3rc2 (RRID:SCR_016216) (Esteban et al., 2019; Esteban, 2022), which is based on Nipype 1.3.1 (RRID:SCR_002502) (Gorgolewski et al., 2011; Esteban et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript describes the preprocessing software used.

claim: Bilateral hippocampal, entorhinal, parahippocampal, and perirhinal cortical ROIs were manually delineated on each participant's high-resolution T1-weighted structural image.
source: Bilateral hippocampal, entorhinal, parahippocampal, and perirhinal cortical ROIs were manually delineated on each participant's high-resolution T1-weighted structural image using established procedures (Olsen et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript describes the ROI definition procedure.

claim: Due to low TSNR, selected scans from 3 participants were excluded from analyses in right EC, and 1 scan from 1 participant was excluded from analyses in left EC.
source: Due to low TSNR (<28), selected scans from 3 participants were excluded from analyses in right EC, and 1 scan from 1 participant was excluded from analyses in left EC.
evidence: The manuscript reports data exclusions based on quality criteria.

claim: Statistical analyses were implemented in R (v3.6.3).
source: Statistical analyses were implemented in R (v3.6.3).
evidence: The manuscript describes the statistical software used.

claim: Linear mixed-effects models were implemented using the lme4 and lmerTest statistical packages.
source: For neural analyses described above, we implemented linear mixed-effects models using the lme4 and lmerTest statistical packages (Bates et al., 2015; Kuznetsova et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript describes the statistical packages used for modeling.

claim: Average univariate activation was included as a regressor to limit the possibility that overall activation differences within an ROI would impact pattern similarity.
source: We included average univariate activation as a regressor to limit the possibility that overall activation differences within an ROI would impact pattern similarity (Ritchey et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript describes a methodological control and cites prior work justifying it.

claim: To control for perceptual similarity between task stimuli, the stimuli were input into vNet, a deep neural network model trained on ecoset.
source: To control for perceptual similarity between task stimuli, we input the stimuli into vNet, a deep neural network model. vNet was trained on ecoset, a large-scale image set containing images from 565 basic level categories (Mehrer et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript describes the method for controlling perceptual similarity.

claim: Raw fMRI data are available on OpenNeuro.
source: Raw fMRI data are available on OpenNeuro.
evidence: The manuscript states where the raw data are available.

claim: Analytical code and behavioral data for reproducing analyses are available at https://github.com/coreyfernandez/RID.
source: Analytical code and behavioral data for reproducing analyses, results, and figures shown in the paper are available at https://github.com/coreyfernandez/RID, (copy archived at swh:1:rev:f4a2d4915f1922c8a74f1f1a86469cf13789abb5; Fernandez, 2023).
evidence: The manuscript states where the code and behavioral data are available.

claim: At the start of the Global Task on Day 2, participants switched to the correct track on 65.78% of across-track trials.
source: At the start of the Global Task on Day 2, participants switched to the correct track on 65.78% (SD = 21.35%) of across-track trials.
evidence: The manuscript reports descriptive statistics from visual examination of navigation routes.

claim: Of trials where participants switched to the correct track at the start of Day 2, they navigated in the correct direction after switching 77.75% of the time.
source: Of those trials, participants navigated in the correct direction after switching 77.75% (SD = 22.52%) of the time.
evidence: The manuscript reports descriptive statistics from visual examination of navigation routes.

claim: By the end of Day 2, participants switched to the correct track on 75.09% of across-track trials.
source: By the end of Day 2, those numbers increased to 75.09% (SD = 20.33%)
evidence: The manuscript reports descriptive statistics showing improvement over Day 2.

claim: By the end of Day 2, participants navigated in the correct direction after switching tracks 85.64% of the time.
source: and 85.64% (SD = 16.91%) respectively.
evidence: The manuscript reports descriptive statistics showing improvement over Day 2.

claim: On Day 3, participants switched to the correct track on 78.36% of across-track trials during the last two runs.
source: Performance continued to improve on Day 3, with participants switching to the correct track on 78.36% (SD = 21.77%) of across-track trials during the last two runs of the Global Navigation Task
evidence: The manuscript reports descriptive statistics showing continued improvement on Day 3.

claim: On Day 3, participants navigated in the correct direction 90.48% of the time after switching tracks.
source: and navigating in the correct direction 90.48% (SD = 10.63%) of the time after switching tracks.
evidence: The manuscript reports descriptive statistics showing continued improvement on Day 3.

claim: Participants learned both the local environments and the global environment, achieving high accuracy and efficiency on within- and across-track trials prior to the final scan on Day 3.
source: Taken together, these data show that participants learned both the local environments (as evidenced by within-track navigation) and the global environment (as evidenced by across-track navigation), achieving high accuracy and efficiency on within- and across-track trials prior to the final scan on Day 3.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the behavioral learning outcomes.

claim: Day 3 data were excluded for two participants (one due to scanner-related issues and one who reported falling asleep during scanning).
source: Day 3 data were excluded for two of these participants (one due to scanner-related issues that prevented data acquisition, and one who reported falling asleep during scanning).
evidence: The manuscript reports data exclusions and reasons.

claim: Global Navigation Task/Day 3 analyses were conducted with 21 participants.
source: Thus, Global Navigation Task/Day 3 analyses were conducted with 21 participants.
evidence: The manuscript reports the sample size for Day 3 analyses.

claim: Participants completed the study in accordance with procedures approved by the Stanford University Institutional Review Board.
source: Thirty-three participants gave informed written consent, in accordance with procedures approved by the Stanford University Institutional Review Board.
evidence: The manuscript reports ethical approval for the study.

claim: The final sample consisted of right-handed participants with normal or corrected-to-normal vision and no self-reported history of psychiatric or neurological disorders.
source: The final sample consisted of 23 right-handed participants (mean age = 22.91 years, SD = 5.03, range 18–35; 14 females) with normal or corrected-to-normal vision and no self-reported history of psychiatric or neurological disorders.
evidence: The manuscript describes inclusion criteria for participants.

claim: Virtual fog limited the distance viewed during Local Navigation, ensuring that no two landmark buildings could be seen at any one time.
source: First-person view from an example training trial (left); virtual fog limited the distance viewed, ensuring that no two landmark buildings could be seen at any one time.
evidence: The manuscript describes a feature of the virtual environment shown in Figure 1b.

claim: During fMRI, participants performed a visual anomaly detection task to ensure they paid close attention to the images.
source: To ensure that participants paid close attention to the images, they performed a visual anomaly detection task in which they were asked to report whether a feature of an image was 'bleached out' on trials when a red fixation cross appeared after image offset (Clarke et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript describes the attention task used during fMRI and cites prior work.

claim: Only a small proportion of stimulus presentations were response trials (~8%) during fMRI.
source: Only a small proportion of stimulus presentations were response trials (~8%).
evidence: The manuscript describes the proportion of response trials in the fMRI task.

claim: Response trials were excluded from all further fMRI analyses.
source: Response trials were excluded from all further analyses.
evidence: The manuscript describes data exclusion criteria for fMRI analysis.

claim: The navigation tasks were developed with Panda3D, a python-based open-source gaming engine, and the PandaEPL library.
source: The navigation tasks were developed with Panda3D (1.9.4), a python-based open-source gaming engine, and the PandaEPL library (Solway et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript describes the software used to develop the navigation tasks.

claim: All 3D models for the virtual environment were created in Maya.
source: All 3D models for the virtual environment were created in Maya (Autodesk, Inc), a 3D graphics program.
evidence: The manuscript describes the software used to create 3D models.

claim: Buildings and fractals were matched for low-level visual features by equating their luminance histograms using the SHINE toolbox.
source: Buildings and fractals were matched for low-level visual features by using the SHINE toolbox in Matlab (version R2015b) to equate their luminance histograms (Willenbockel et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript describes the method for controlling visual features and cites the toolbox.

claim: Movement during navigation was fixed along the centerline of the paths and movement speed was held constant.
source: Movement was fixed along the centerline of the paths and movement speed was held constant.
evidence: The manuscript describes constraints on participant movement during navigation.

claim: Traveling around one individual path required approximately 30 seconds.
source: Traveling around one individual path required approximately 30 s.
evidence: The manuscript provides timing information about navigation.

claim: During the Local Navigation Task, participants navigated from every goal on a track to every other goal on that track, several times.
source: In total, participants navigated from every goal on a track to every other goal on that track, several times.
evidence: The manuscript describes the comprehensiveness of navigation experience.

claim: Track order during the Local Navigation Task was randomized and counterbalanced across participants.
source: Track order was randomized and counterbalanced across participants.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental design to control for order effects.

claim: During the Global Navigation Task, 30 of 90 test trials required participants to navigate to a goal along the track on which they were already located.
source: For 30 of 90 test trials, participants were cued to navigate to a goal along the track on which they were already located.
evidence: The manuscript describes the trial composition of the Global Navigation Task.

claim: During the Global Navigation Task, 60 of 90 test trials required participants to navigate to a different track.
source: For the other 60 test trials, participants were required to navigate to a different track.
evidence: The manuscript describes the trial composition of the Global Navigation Task.

claim: The first 6 TRs in each fMRI run were removed prior to analysis.
source: Prior to fMRI analyses, we removed the first 6 TRs in each run.
evidence: The manuscript describes preprocessing steps for fMRI data.

claim: GLMs yielded estimates of voxel-level brain activity for each stimulus during odd and even runs of each scan session.
source: GLMs yielded estimates of voxel-level brain activity for each stimulus during odd and even runs of each scan session.
evidence: The manuscript describes the output of the GLM analysis.

claim: Modeling was performed with SPM12 and custom Matlab routines.
source: Modeling was performed with SPM12 (Wellcome Trust Centre for Neuroimaging) and custom Matlab (vR2017b) routines.
evidence: The manuscript describes the software used for fMRI modeling.

claim: A visual ROI defined by FreeSurfer's automated segmentation procedure was used as a control for the analyses.
source: Finally, we used a visual ROI defined by FreeSurfer's automated segmentation procedure as a control for our analyses. The mask for this ROI was defined as a conjunction of FreeSurfer's pericalcarine and calcarine sulcus regions in both hemispheres.
evidence: The manuscript describes the control ROI used in analyses.

claim: Pattern similarity analyses were conducted in Python (v2.7).
source: Pattern similarity analyses were conducted in Python (v2.7).
evidence: The manuscript describes the software used for pattern similarity analysis.

claim: No explicit power analysis was conducted to predetermine sample size.
source: No explicit power analysis was conducted to predetermine sample size, but we aimed to collect 30 participants for the multi-day study.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges the absence of a formal power analysis.

claim: The present sample size (n = 23) is comparable to that of prior fMRI studies examining mnemonic representations that did not scan across three consecutive days.
source: The present sample size (n = 23) is comparable to that of prior fMRI studies examining mnemonic representations that did not scan across three consecutive days (e.g. Chanales et al., 2017; Deuker et al., 2016; Tompary and Davachi, 2017; Zheng et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript justifies the sample size by comparison to prior studies.

claim: Correlations (the dependent variable) were Fisher transformed to follow a normal distribution.
source: Correlations, our dependent variable, were Fisher transformed to follow a normal distribution.
evidence: The manuscript describes a statistical transformation applied to the data.

claim: Models were estimated using a restricted maximum likelihood (REML) approach.
source: Models were estimated using a restricted maximum likelihood (REML) approach.
evidence: The manuscript describes the estimation method for statistical models.

claim: The false discovery rate was controlled using the Benjamini and Hochberg method.
